prompt: Food-delivery orders in Bengaluru dropped 15% week over week. Find out why.

context.setup: You're the PM for the consumer app at a food-delivery company.
hiddenFacts: Metric definition if asked: completed orders; placed orders also fell. Other cities: flat. Bengaluru only.
Platform split if asked: Android down 24%, iOS flat, web flat. App version if asked: Android v5.2 released Monday to 100% of users.
Funnel if asked: sessions flat, menu views flat, checkout-to-payment conversion down sharply.
Root cause (reveal only if the candidate narrows to it): a payment SDK update in v5.2 fails for one popular bank's UPI handle.
External if asked: no competitor campaign, weather normal, no holiday.

expectedStructure: Clarify metric definition, time window, how sudden
Check data or tracking issues first
Internal versus external factors
Segment: geo, platform, app version, cohort, restaurant side
Funnel to locate the break
Prioritise hypotheses, verify, immediate mitigation and long-term fix

rubricHints.structure: Systematic narrowing: definition, data validity, internal or external, segments, funnel.
rubricHints.userFocus: Asks which users are affected (platform, bank) rather than guessing about all users.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Orders hypotheses by likelihood and ease of checking; checks cheap ones first.
rubricHints.metrics: Uses the funnel and segment cuts as evidence, not guesses.
rubricHints.communication: States the root cause, the evidence and the next action crisply.

commonPitfalls: Never asks for platform or version split
Stops at the root cause without mitigation

followUpSeeds.text: You haven't split by platform or app version. What would you look at there?
Of the hypotheses you listed, which do you check first, and why that order?
Say sessions are flat but orders fell. Where in the funnel do you look, and what would you expect to see?
You've found it. What do you tell your VP in two sentences, and what happens today?
New information: {variant}. How does that change your investigation?

market: the drop is across all metros, not just Bengaluru
constraint: you have no access to engineering for 48 hours
your analytics pipeline was also changed last week
user: the drop is only among new users in their first week

prompt: Average watch time per user on a short-video app fell 10% in a week, but daily active users went up. What's going on?

hiddenFacts: Change if asked: a new recommendation model rolled out to 50% of Indian users last Tuesday.
Treatment group: more sessions per user, shorter sessions; new-creator content share up.
A Diwali campaign brought in many new, light users the same week.
Both effects are real; the candidate should separate mix shift from per-user behaviour.

expectedStructure: Clarify the metric (average per DAU?) and the window
Recognise a ratio metric: numerator and denominator move separately
Mix shift (new light users) versus behaviour change (model rollout)
Segment by new versus existing users and treatment versus control
Conclude whether it's a problem and what to do

rubricHints.userFocus: Separates new light users from existing heavy users.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Separates 'is this bad?' from 'why did it move?'.
rubricHints.metrics: Proposes cohort-level watch time (existing users only) and treatment versus control.

commonPitfalls: Assumes engagement dropped without checking mix

followUpSeeds.text: DAU went up. Could the average fall without any single user watching less? How would you check?
There was also a model rollout to half of users. How do you separate the two effects?
Is a 10% drop here actually a problem? What would make you roll the model back?
Suppose {variant}. What now?

constraint: there is no control group, the model went to 100%
user: the drop is concentrated in users over 35
market: it's happening only in Indonesia, where you launched three months ago

prompt: Late-delivery complaints for an e-commerce marketplace doubled in Hyderabad this month, but average delivery time hasn't changed. Why?

hiddenFacts: Complaints are concentrated on orders tagged 'Express'.
The promise-date algorithm was changed this month to show earlier promised dates to lift conversion.
Actual delivery times are unchanged; the share delivered after the promised date rose from 6% to 14%.

expectedStructure: Notice the paradox: complaints are about expectation versus actual
Define 'late' relative to the promise and check complaint tagging
Segment by order type, seller, courier, pin code
Find the promise-date change; quantify; trade-off conversion versus trust
Recommendation and guardrail (on-time-to-promise %)

rubricHints.structure: Resolves the paradox by redefining 'late' relative to the promise.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Weighs conversion gain against complaints, returns and trust.
rubricHints.metrics: Proposes on-time-versus-promise rate and distribution, not averages.

followUpSeeds.text: The average is flat. What other view of delivery time could still explain more complaints?
What changed on our side this month that could affect what customers expect?

Assume instead that {variant}. Where do you look?

constraint: the promise-date algorithm did not change
market: it's all cities, but only for one courier partner

prompt: Ride-hailing cancellations rose 20% in one city over two weeks. Find out why.

expectedStructure: Clarify which cancellations (driver or rider) and time window

rubricHints.metrics: Cuts by trip length or flag exposure as evidence.

prompt: Seller sign-ups for an online marketplace dropped 30% in a month, though traffic to the sign-up page rose. Why?

rubricHints.prioritisation: Orders by evidence, weighs policy change against growth.
